source.title: Self-Supervision is All You Need for Solving Rubik's Cube

record.file_problem: none; the full paper is present.
record.tranche_reason: It applies a language-model scaling-law formulation to a Rubik’s Cube solver, a different task and training regime, and reports scaling and downstream results.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws and adopts Hoffmann et al.’s parametric form; cited results are not recorded as rows. Its own scaling sweep and downstream solver evaluations are recorded. The loss values in the scaling plots are not reported numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The paper fits Hoffmann et al.'s parametric loss law to 36 of its own Rubik's Cube solver models (non-language, self-supervised scramble prediction). It derives a compute-optimal N/D split and evaluates the three largest models downstream. These are its own results in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the solver scales with parameters and data, scaling improves downstream solving, and the time-efficiency benefit of model size plateaus. Also, the fitted split is roughly equal, in line with Hoffmann et al.
record.recipe_differences: Adopts Hoffmann et al.’s power-law formulation and compute-optimal allocation approach, but applies it to a Rubik’s Cube solver rather than an autoregressive language model. It uses C ≈ 3ND for dense DNNs and fits validation loss by minimizing mean squared error with L-BFGS.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that temporal benefits from increasing model size may plateau depending on the execution environment; in their single-GPU setup, increasing training data rather than model parameters would be beneficial for temporal efficiency.
record.problems: The scaling evidence is from one task and 36 fitted models; plotted validation-loss and downstream results lack reported numerical values and uncertainty estimates. The paper reports one fitting procedure rather than sensitivity tests across fitting choices.

untested.parts: Models were scaled progressively using fits on smaller runs, but the final model's predicted vs observed loss is not reported.
No language-model allocation; the Rubik's allocation is recorded under V5.
No shape comparison at fixed N.
'Predictably' is not tested: there is no fit of downstream metric against compute or loss, only 3 models, no language tasks.
No sensitivity to fitting choices and no comparison of laws.

missing.what: Time-based downstream efficiency saturation is not a separate row; it is described in text and Fig. 6 right.

record.verdict_notes: The main paper is a Rubik's solver method; the scaling section is secondary. The fitted exponents actually favour data slightly (0.57 vs 0.43 for D vs N), which the authors summarise as equal. No uncertainty is reported for the fit.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss in language models.
It does not report a direct comparison of loss predictions fitted on small runs with observed losses of much larger runs.
Tests allocation for a Rubik’s Cube solver, not language-model parameters and tokens; it does not compare Kaplan et al.’s allocation trend.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests a power-law scaling form on a Rubik’s Cube solver; does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests downstream Rubik’s Cube solving outcomes across scaled models, not language-model tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss.

It reports one fitting setup and its fitted parameters, but does not test sensitivity to setup or fitting choices, compare competing published laws, or report curves bending away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Rubik’s Cube solver DNN (36-model scaling sweep)
rows.size_stated: varied; final model approximately 119 million parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fit a two-variable power-law loss function to validation-loss observations across model size and training-data volume.

conditions.value: 36 total; 30 random low-budget models initiated the experiment
1.4 × 10^13 to 3.2 × 10^15 for the initial 30 models; final model at 5.14 × 10^19 FLOPs

rows.measure: Validation loss as model parameters and training data volume increase; fitted loss-law parameters
rows.value: Validation loss diminishes as either model size or training data volume increases (Figure 5); fitted E = 0.892, A = 4.0, B = 6.2, α = 0.178, and β = 0.134.
rows.note: The trend is described in the text, but individual loss values are only plotted. The final model used approximately 119 million parameters and 144 billion states (7.2 billion examples).
rows.check: Fit quality, residuals and per-model losses are not reported; the power-law form is assumed (Eq. 2) and fitted, not compared against alternatives. Architecture also differs from Section 4: uniform width, no residuals, half-turn metric.

rows.subject: Rubik’s Cube solver DNN (fitted compute-optimal allocation)
rows.operation_detail: Estimate compute-optimal model-size and training-data allocation from the fitted loss function.

conditions.value: L-BFGS; initial-value grid for A, B, α, and β

rows.measure: Estimated allocation of model size and training data for compute-optimal performance
rows.value: α : β = 0.57 : 0.43; the authors say model size and training data should scale in roughly equal proportions. Final model: C = 5.14 × 10^19 FLOPs, N ≈ 119 million parameters, D ≈ 144 billion states (7.2 billion examples).
rows.note: The reported exponents and allocation are from the fitted Rubik’s Cube solver scaling law.
rows.check: V3 names language-model parameter and token allocation; this is an MLP Rubik's solver, so the row bears on V5 only. The fitted exponents imply N_opt∝C^0.43 and D_opt∝C^0.57, so data grows slightly faster; the authors call this 'roughly equal'. The split comes from one fit, not a test of stability across budgets.

rows.subject: Rubik’s Cube solver, C = 6.12e17 FLOPs
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate a scaled solver on the DeepCubeA Rubik’s Cube dataset using IDA*-prepared optimal solutions.

conditions.value: solution length and optimality as a function of node count and time

rows.note: One of the three largest models compared. The text describes the overall scaling trend, not separate numerical values for this model.
rows.check: Figure-only; only 3 models. Improvement is in nodes and optimality, while time-based efficiency saturates.

relationships.condition: Rubik's Cube solver MLPs, compute ~1.4e13 to 5.14e19 FLOPs, 36 models
relationships.reason: Validation loss falls with N and D, and a Chinchilla-form law fits (α=0.178, β=0.134), giving a near-equal compute-optimal split (r1, r2). Fit quality is not reported.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss fit a Chinchilla-form law with α = 0.178 and β = 0.134, implying a near-equal compute-optimal allocation.

relationships.condition: Three largest Rubik's solvers, node-count-based solution length and optimality
relationships.reason: Higher training compute gives shorter, more optimal solutions with fewer nodes (Fig. 6). There are only 3 models and the evidence is figure-only (r3–r5).
relationships.display_finding: Across three models, higher training compute produced shorter, more optimal solutions while requiring fewer search nodes.

relationships.condition: Time-based (wall-clock) downstream efficiency on a single T4 GPU
relationships.reason: Authors report near-saturating benefit of model size for temporal performance, due to inference latency (r3–r5, Fig. 6 right).
relationships.display_finding: Wall-clock performance gains nearly saturate as model size increases because inference latency offsets the benefits.
